articles.title: Here’s How to Adult the Right Way and Get Your Life on Track, According to Your Zodiac Sign
articles.content:
As the first sign of the zodiac, you’re a natural starter, Aries. Ruled by energetic Mars, you’re at your best when there’s a challenge to conquer, a goal to chase or someplace new to go. Unfortunately, adult life involves an awful lot of maintenance. Paying bills, doing laundry and having the same meeting every Tuesday can make an Aries want to crawl out of their skin.
If you’re in a rut, don’t try to transform yourself into someone who loves routine. Instead, give yourself something new to conquer. At work, volunteer for a project that stretches your skills, pitch an idea or set a goal with a finish line you can actually see. If your relationship feels stale, plan a date that gets both of you off the couch. Take a boxing class, go hiking or make a reservation at that restaurant across town you’ve been dying to try.
You can even turn mundane chores into a competition with yourself. Set a timer for 30 minutes, put on some music and see how much you can knock out before the buzzer. And remember: Your ability to compete in the financial world should inspire you too.
The pitfall? You can mistake boredom for failure. Before quitting a job, abandoning a goal or deciding a relationship has run its course, ask yourself whether you really want out or simply need a fresh challenge within the life you already have.
Taurus is an earth sign ruled by Venus, the planet associated with beauty, pleasure and love, and you need a life that feels good in the real, tangible world. A beautiful home, delicious food, financial security and people you can count on aren’t frivolous extras for you—they’re what you need to feel grounded. So when life gets off track, start with your physical environment. Clean out the refrigerator, buy fresh sheets, cook yourself a real meal or finally deal with that pile of stuff you’ve been stepping around for three months. Don’t underestimate how much changing your surroundings can change your mood. And pay special attention to color palettes.
Money is another important piece of the Taurus puzzle. You crave security, so vague financial goals can create unnecessary anxiety. Pick something concrete: Pay off a credit card, save a specific amount or set aside money for a vacation you can already picture yourself taking. Automating your savings can help, because once a good Taurus habit takes root, it tends to stay there.
The same goes for relationships. You value loyalty, but that can sometimes keep you in situations long after their expiration date. Your famous stubborn streak is wonderful when you’re building something worthwhile; it’s less useful when you’re hanging on simply because change feels uncomfortable. Ask yourself: Does this still make my life better, or am I just used to it?
Quick-thinking Gemini is ruled by Mercury, the planet associated with communication, and your mind needs stimulation. You’re curious, witty and full of ideas. But when every day starts looking exactly like the one before it, your energy can take a nosedive. Your reset word is variety. If work feels dull, ask to take on a different responsibility, work somewhere new for an afternoon or schedule lunch with a colleague who always gets your brain buzzing. If you’ve been thinking about taking a class, learning a language or starting a hobby, do it. Your curiosity isn’t a distraction from your adult life; it’s one of the things that keeps you engaged with it!
Your relationships need variety as well. Call the friend you haven’t talked to in six months. Plan a weekend road trip. Ask your partner a question you’ve never asked before. Gemini is the communicator of the zodiac, and talking things out often helps you figure out what you actually want.
But watch your tendency to scatter your energy: 12 exciting ideas can quickly become 12 unfinished projects. Choose one thing you want to change this month, and follow it through before chasing the next shiny object.
Home really is where the heart is for Cancer. You’re sensitive, intuitive and deeply connected to family and the people you consider family, so when your home life feels chaotic, everything else can feel off too. Begin your reset there. You don’t need a magazine-worthy makeover. Clear one room that’s become cluttered, create a comfortable place to eat dinner, or establish a little corner where you can read, think or drink your morning coffee without interruption. If you work remotely, make sure you have a dedicated workspace so your job doesn’t ooze into every inch of your sanctuary.
Cancer also has a tremendous instinct for nurturing others. That makes you the person others call when they’re upset, sick or simply need someone to listen. Yes, it’s lovely in many ways, but being everyone’s emotional emergency room can leave you depleted. Spend time working out, or head to a spa for a reset.
Try putting one appointment with yourself on your calendar every week and treating it as seriously as you would a commitment to someone you love. And if you’re worried about money, create a small emergency fund, even if you start with just a few dollars every week. Security gives Cancer room to breathe.
One word of warning: Don’t confuse caring with caretaking. Sometimes the most loving thing you can say is: “I can’t do that today.”
Leo is ruled by the Sun, and you’re here to shine. That doesn’t mean every Leo wants to become famous, of course. It means you need opportunities to express yourself, create and feel that what you contribute actually matters.
If you’ve been going through the motions, ask yourself where you’ve become an understudy in your own life. At work, stop quietly doing excellent work and hoping somebody notices. Speak up in the meeting, apply for the promotion or show your boss what you’ve accomplished. In your personal life, revive something that makes you feel creative, whether that’s singing, decorating, dancing or hosting a fabulous dinner.
Relationships are important to warmhearted Leo, and appreciation matters too. But rather than stewing because somebody hasn’t noticed everything you do, tell them what you need. And make sure you’re giving that appreciation back.
The pitfall you need to watch out for? Looking outside yourself for applause. Likes, compliments and recognition feel wonderful, but they can’t be your only fuel source. Pick one goal that would make you proud, even if nobody else knew you accomplished it. That’s the kind of spotlight that never gets switched off. To keep that perspective top of mind, put an inspirational quote on your fridge to light you up every day.
Virgo is the gardener in my astrology system, and that image tells you a lot about how this practical earth sign operates. You’re brilliant at tending things, whether that means improving a project, organizing a household, helping a friend or figuring out why the dishwasher is making that weird noise. The trouble begins when everything starts looking like it needs improvement, including you.
If your life feels overwhelming, resist the urge to overhaul the whole thing. Pick three things that genuinely need your attention. Maybe it’s making a doctor’s appointment you’ve postponed, creating a workable monthly budget and clearing your desk so you can actually see it again. Then stop. You do not need a 47-item self-improvement plan.
At work, decide which tasks actually move a project forward instead of polishing every detail. At home, create simple routines that eliminate recurring annoyances. Put your keys in the same place. Schedule automatic bill payments. Make a basic meal plan. And in relationships, remember that the people you love aren’t projects. Sometimes they want your company, not your excellent suggestions.
Warning: Watch out for perfectionism masquerading as productivity. “Better” is often good enough. Let the garden grow.
Libra is the zodiac’s great relationship sign. Ruled by Venus, you have a natural ability to see another person’s point of view, create harmony and make people feel comfortable. Those are fantastic adulting skills, right up until you become so busy considering everyone else that you lose track of what you want. So your reset begins with a decision. Choose something you’ve been endlessly weighing, and give yourself a deadline. Which vacation should you take? Do you want the new job? Which sofa should you buy? Gather the information you need, sleep on it and decide. No additional committee meetings required.
This applies to relationships too. Before asking your partner, best friend, mother and group chat what they think, ask yourself first. Write down your answer if you need to. You might be surprised by how quickly it comes. At work, practice stating your opinion before hearing everyone else’s. With money, create a personal spending category that you control without anybody else’s input.
Your gift for compromise is precious, but compromise only works when you bring your own desires to the table. Otherwise, you aren’t meeting someone halfway; you’re simply walking over to their side.
Scorpio is the shaman in my astrology system, since this sign is associated with transformation, depth and rebirth. You have a remarkable ability to reinvent yourself, but first you have to be willing to let something die. Don’t panic—we’re talking metaphorically!
If you feel stuck in life, take inventory of what you’ve outgrown. Is there a friendship that exists mostly because you’ve known each other forever? A job that once challenged you but now drains you? A closet full of possessions belonging to a version of yourself you left behind years ago? Pick one area and purge. Delete the apps you never use. Donate the clothes. Cancel the subscription. Have the conversation you’ve been avoiding. Update the résumé. Money deserves the same fearless examination. Look at your accounts, debts and spending instead of avoiding whatever makes you uncomfortable. Scorpio does surprisingly well when the truth is out in the open because then you can do something about it.
Just don’t confuse transformation with destruction. You don’t have to burn down your whole life to change it. Sometimes removing one dead branch is enough to let new growth through. And for you, the most expansive growth will be in your romantic relationships.
Sagittarius is the explorer of the zodiac. Ruled by Jupiter, you thrive on adventure, learning and the feeling that life contains possibilities you haven’t discovered yet. When you feel trapped, your first instinct may be to book a ticket somewhere far away. And if you can afford the trip, go! Travel can be genuinely restorative for Sagittarius.
But expansion doesn’t require an airport. Take a class in something you know nothing about. Visit a neighborhood you’ve never explored. Go to a museum alone. Invite someone with a completely different background to lunch. At work, look for opportunities to teach, travel, present or acquire a new skill. Your enthusiasm returns when your world gets bigger.
Money requires a little more discipline. Your optimism can persuade you that future-you will somehow take care of whatever present-you puts on the credit card. Create a separate travel or adventure fund, and use that money guilt-free. In relationships, make sure freedom goes both ways. You need room to roam, but so do the people you love.
Remember, though: The answer doesn’t always lie somewhere else. Before escaping your current life, see whether you can grow within it.
Capricorn, you are built for adulting. You’re ambitious, practical and naturally aware that worthwhile things take time. Give you a mountain and you’ll start figuring out the route to the summit while everyone else is still discussing footwear. But capable Capricorn can end up carrying far too much.
If your life needs a reset, choose your most important mountain. Maybe you want to buy a home, change careers, get out of debt or finally finish a degree. Write down the goal, break it into smaller milestones and put actual dates beside them. You’re at your best when progress is measurable and when you work one step at a time, in a grounded way. Then look at everything else you’re doing and decide what can wait. Being responsible doesn’t mean volunteering to carry every responsibility in sight. This is especially important in families and relationships, where Capricorn can quietly become the CEO, CFO and facilities manager. Delegate. Ask for help. Let someone else make dinner badly.
Your pitfall is postponing happiness until you reach the next milestone. Schedule pleasure with the same seriousness you schedule work. There will always be another mountain.
Independent Aquarius is the zodiac’s innovator. You’re interested in what’s next, what’s possible and how things could work differently. So why are you still living according to a rule you stopped believing in five years ago? You are an air sign, and your inventive mind is your greatest gift. Look around for a “should.” You should have this kind of career. You should spend weekends this way. You should own a house by a certain age. You should have a particular kind of relationship. Then ask yourself who made that rule.
At work, experiment with technology or a new system that eliminates something tedious. If your schedule isn’t working, rearrange it. In your social life, seek out people who share your interests rather than maintaining friendships solely because you’ve known someone forever.
Aquarius is also associated with groups and community, so if you’ve become isolated, join something. Volunteer for a cause, find a local organization or seek out people who are fascinated by the same wonderfully obscure thing you are.
Just don’t rebel for the sake of rebellion. A conventional solution isn’t automatically a bad one. Keep the rules that work; toss the ones that don’t.
Dreamy Pisces is imaginative, intuitive and creative. You can picture possibilities other people don’t see, which is an extraordinary gift. The adulting problem arrives when those possibilities remain beautiful little movies playing inside your head. Your reset is to make one dream concrete. Want to write a book? Set a weekly page goal. Dreaming of Paris? Open a vacation account and automatically deposit money into it every payday. Want a different career? Spend one hour this week researching what training you would actually need. Creativity becomes powerful when you give it a container.
Your environment matters too. Pisces absorbs atmosphere easily, so create spaces that help you feel calm and inspired. Music, water, art, meditation or simply taking a walk without your phone can help you clear out other people’s noise and hear your own thoughts again. And remember: Relationships require boundaries. Your empathy can make somebody else’s crisis feel like your responsibility. Before rushing in to rescue someone, ask whether they actually need your help and whether you genuinely have the energy to give it.
Your pitfall is waiting for inspiration, rescue or the perfect moment. Put one date on the calendar, and take one practical step. Dreams need feet.

articles.title: Our Readers Share the Things They Can’t Live Without—And They’re Totally Relatable
articles.content:
We all have that one thing we’d hate to be without. Maybe it’s tucked into a kitchen drawer or sitting within arm’s reach at all times. It might not look particularly important to anyone else, but to us? Absolutely essential. So we asked our readers to share the things they simply can’t live without, and their answers prove that sometimes the most ordinary objects carry the best stories.
The list ahead includes practical picks, sentimental treasures and a few items we didn’t see coming. Some will make perfect sense the second you read them. Others may have you thinking, Wait, that’s what you can’t live without?! And they will definitely all prompt you to consider of your own must-haves.
Read on to discover the nostalgic and wonderfully relatable things our readers can’t live without, along with the heartwarming stories that make them so special.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more true stories, fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.
My needle and thread. They’re two things, but one doesn’t work without the other. My hands are always busy creating: in my sewing room, in the car, on vacation, in waiting rooms. But the most special times with my needle and thread were in the evenings when my late husband and I would sit in our chairs and watch TV while I sewed. He was always the biggest fan of whatever I was working on. After he died, it took a while before I could pick up my needle and thread. I’m creating again, but tears come easy when I look at his chair, and I still hold up what I’m working on and turn to his chair to “show him.” —Steven Cook, Eagle River, Alaska
As long as there are ideas and mistakes and I have the ability to change my mind, I need pencils with good erasers. I keep them in my workroom, my car and my crossword book, and by my bed. I use them to keep my changing calendar of dinner dates and my grandson’s baseball games, make to-do lists, jot down promises. A pencil allows me to be an imaginative, but fallible, human being. —Mirjam Spaar, Severna Park, Maryland
Many people say they can’t live without coffee, but I take it to the extreme. I carry a coffee maker with me wherever I travel. When I worked as a flight attendant, I spent many nights in hotels and couldn’t risk going without that morning cup. My fix—no pun intended—came from the smallest coffee maker that I could pack into my crew bag. It was a single-brew machine that worked magic every morning. —Amber Jensen-Veney, Blairsville, Georgia
I’ve worn heavy black eyeliner ever since I was a teenager. I was enthralled by characters on shows like Bewitched, Star Trek and I Dream of Jeannie. My kids always told me to tone it down. articles.title: Is It Really Rude to Leave a One-Star Review?
articles.content:
About 10 years ago, my husband and I loaded our kids into the car and drove to what was billed as a destination family resort with an indoor water park. The ads promised a magical, kid-friendly escape worth the drive. We booked it without a second thought. We should have had at least one second thought.
When we arrived, the parking lot was empty. Not “offseason quiet” empty— more like “the last guests left under mysterious circumstances and nobody came after them” empty. The lobby carpet was torn up in patches. The hallways were dim and echoey. And the indoor water park, advertised with glistening slides and splashing families, consisted of exactly one broken slide standing in an otherwise empty pool. My kids’ faces broke my heart. The concierge was pleasant enough. She advised us to just wander the halls and pick whatever room looked good to us. So we chose the least creepy option, pushed the bureau in front of the door before bed, and left first thing in the morning.
That day, I wrote the only one-star review I have ever left in my life. It was two pages long and included photos. I went with equal parts scathing and cautionary. A few months later, I went back to see if the hotel had responded. Instead, I found that it had permanently closed. Part of me wonders whether my review was the final nail in the coffin.
But was leaving it actually the right thing to do? I’ve been thinking about it ever since, because the etiquette of negative reviews is genuinely murky, and the stakes can be higher than most of us realize.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more etiquette, tech, holiday tips, fun facts, humor and travel all week long.
The most obvious argument for a negative review is that you were asked and the service was truly terrible. Every time you visit a business, Google, Yelp, Amazon and everyone else wants to know how it went. We’ve built an entire consumer infrastructure around the premise that honest feedback is valuable.
So staying silent when you have had a genuinely terrible experience seems, if anything, like failing your civic duty. There weren’t any reviews of the hotel when I booked our trip (which should have been my first red flag), and they would have been so useful. The data backs this up: 94% of consumers say a negative review has convinced them to avoid a business.
Reviews are how strangers protect one another. When a hotel advertises a water park and delivers one sad slide in a drained pool, that’s not a minor inconvenience—it’s actually a misrepresentation. Plus, honest negative reviews can benefit businesses. A consistent pattern of one-star complaints about cold food is information that the management can act on. Silence isn’t kindness; it’s useless.
OK, but … a single one-star review can also do lasting, disproportionate damage to a small business. Especially if it’s exaggerated (as can happen when you write in the heat of the moment). A landmark Harvard Business School study found that a one-star drop on Yelp translates to a 5% to 9% revenue loss. And industry estimates suggest it takes roughly 40 positive customer experiences to claw back the reputational damage of just one negative review. For a small business operating on thin margins, that revenue loss could represent payroll, rent and the owner’s ability to keep the lights on.
Also, many of the issues stem from circumstances that no individual employee created. One terrible visit, driven by a broken system or an understaffed night, may not represent the whole story. Leaving a permanent, public indictment based on a single bad day can feel less like accountability and more like collateral damage.
It’s also worth noting that online review culture has developed a genuinely ugly side that has nothing to do with honest consumer feedback and everything to do with online bullying.
In 2025, a James Beard–nominated San Francisco chef found his restaurant review-bombed into closure after a dispute with a TikToker went viral. Hundreds of thousands of people who had never set foot in his restaurant, never tasted his food, never interacted with a single member of his staff flooded his Google page with one-star reviews because an influencer told them to. His employees were laid off, he lost his livelihood and his restaurant closed. And that’s just one example of many.
This is not etiquette; this is bullying. And it is one of the worst things happening in online culture right now. A review is supposed to be your honest account of your own experience. The moment you leave a one-star review for a business you’ve never visited, you’re not holding anyone accountable. You are, however, weaponizing hate. A review platform is not a pitchfork, and treating it like one doesn’t make you an activist—it makes you incredibly rude.
Here’s what I’ve settled on: A one-star review is appropriate when the problem was systemic, significant and likely to happen to the next person. Not because your server was having a hard shift. Not because your food arrived slightly cold during a Saturday-night rush. When there is genuine misrepresentation involved or consistent, recurring failures, you are not being rude. And I will say that given this rubric, I’ve never left another one-star review.
If you’re going to leave a one-star review, there are a few practical rules. Be specific, not mean. Describe what happened rather than what you think of the person who served you. Don’t write it in the heat of your emotions. And before you post anything, consider calling the business directly. A surprising number of problems get resolved this way, and a business willing to make it right deserves the opportunity. If they don’t respond, you will feel considerably better about that one star. Leaving a one-star review is not inherently rude—but the bar should be meaningfully higher than “I was mildly inconvenienced on a Tuesday.”
My two-page review of the haunted water park hotel, with its empty pool and bureau-against-the-door energy? One hundred percent warranted. I regret nothing. If I saved even one family from driving three hours to stand in a dark lobby choosing a room like contestants on Squid Game, that was a public service.

articles.title: Swanville, Minnesota, Made a Promise to Give Scholarships to Every Student—And Transformed Generations of Kids
articles.content:
When Brody Kircher stepped up to receive his high school diploma and head off to college, he knew that the people of Swanville, Minnesota, would have his back. The only question was exactly how many dollars they would put in his pocket.
“I expected maybe $4,000,” he says. But the actual amount Kircher received was much more than he guessed: $6,000. “This community really comes together,” he says. “They’re trying to make sure that everyone has a chance. We’re kind of spoiled, honestly. In a bigger place, they wouldn’t be able to do it for everybody.”
For graduates of Swanville High School, there’s never any suspense about who’ll get a scholarship: If you apply, you’ll get one. And in this tiny town deep in Minnesota farm country, where the class of 2026 numbered just 22 students, almost every senior applies.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more of the Nicest Places in America, heartwarming stories, fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.
Known as Dollars for Scholars, what started as a modest effort to help local students has evolved into a deep-rooted institution that now gives away about $100,000 in scholarships a year. Recipients can use the money for almost anything: college, trade school or continuing life skills for special education students. The program is backed by a year-round fundraising effort that includes bingo games, poinsettia sales, and weekly “meat raffles,” where locals buy chances to fill their freezers.
